claims.text: Thirteen representatives from Denmark, England, France, Germany, Holland, Switzerland and the United States conferred in Paris from January 11 to 16, 1960. Before the meeting Naur had worked out a completely new draft report, and the conference adopted that draft as the basis for its report.

source.title: ALGOL 60: the Paris conference of January 1960, its attendees, and the naming of Backus-Naur form at Knuth’s suggestion

claims.text: Naur was drawn into the international discussions as editor of the ALGOL Bulletin, was selected as a member of the European language design group in November 1959, and in that capacity served as editor of the report resulting from the Paris meeting.

source.title: ALGOL 60: the Paris conference of January 1960, its attendees, and the naming of Backus-Naur form at Knuth’s suggestion

claims.text: The attendees included Bauer, Rutishauser, Samelson, Vauquois, van Wijngaarden and Woodger from Europe, and Backus, Green, Katz, McCarthy, Perlis and Wegstein from the United States.

source.title: ALGOL 60: the Paris conference of January 1960, its attendees, and the naming of Backus-Naur form at Knuth’s suggestion

claims.text: The notation Backus had devised for the earlier ALGOL specification was revised and expanded by Naur, and at Knuth’s suggestion it was renamed Backus-Naur form.

source.title: ALGOL 60: the Paris conference of January 1960, its attendees, and the naming of Backus-Naur form at Knuth’s suggestion

claims.text: The report defines blocks delimited by begin and end, procedures that may be invoked recursively, procedures nested within one another, and lexical scope, in which a name refers to the declaration enclosing it in the text.

source.title: Naur, P. (ed.), Report on the Algorithmic Language ALGOL 60, Communications of the ACM 3(5), May 1960

claims.text: The language as officially defined contains no input or output facilities, so implementations supplied their own, in largely incompatible ways.

source.title: Naur, P. (ed.), Report on the Algorithmic Language ALGOL 60, Communications of the ACM 3(5), May 1960

claims.text: Hoare wrote of it, in his 1980 Turing Award lecture: "Here is a language so far ahead of its time that it was not only an improvement on its predecessors but also on nearly all its successors."

source.title: Hoare, C. A. R., The Emperor’s Old Clothes, 1980 Turing Award Lecture, Communications of the ACM 24(2), February 1981

claims.text: It gave rise to CPL, Simula, BCPL, B, Pascal and C.

source.title: ALGOL 60: the Paris conference of January 1960, its attendees, and the naming of Backus-Naur form at Knuth’s suggestion

claims.text: The immediately preceding attempt at a vendor-independent language, COBOL, was specified in English words for commands, on the reasoning that the specification should be readable by people who do not program.

source.title: Sammet, J. E., The Early History of COBOL, in History of Programming Languages, ACM SIGPLAN Notices, 1978

beats.broke: there was no way to state what a language was, so each language existed only as whatever its compiler happened to accept
beats.fix: a formal grammar for the syntax and a published report as the definition, plus block structure, lexical scope and recursion
beats.cost: the report defines no input or output, so every implementation added its own and the programs did not move
beats.interview: why the notation for describing the language mattered more than the language
